articles.title: Twenty-eight days in, the war began: Malaysia Airlines' CEO on fuel shocks, full planes and the India bet
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Nasaruddin A Bakar, president, and group CEO of Malaysia Aviation Group, took charge just before before the West Asia crisis began.
articles.body: MUMBAI:Nasaruddin A Bakar, president, and group CEO of Malaysia Aviation Group, took charge just before before the West Asia crisis began. Seven months on, he talks to the Times of India about running a thin-margin airline through a crisis, why India matters more than ever and what happens when the visa-free window closes.Nasaruddin A Bakar had barely found his CEO chair at Malaysia Aviation Group when the world's most important aviation corridor shut down."Twenty-eight days after I sat in the seat, the war started," the group CEO says, with the dry humour of a man who has since had time to reflect on it.The West Asia crisis that erupted at the end of February did what such conflicts do to airlines. It closed airspace, stranded passengers, and sent fuel prices soaring. Eight months on, fuel prices are nowhere near cooling. For the new CEO, the first month was about survival and logistics rather than strategy."The first two weeks were about how we manage three things: our people over there, our passengers over there, and our assets in the Middle East," he says. He spent much of that time with his team, trying to understand what was happening on the ground.The fuel bill nobody budgets for"War happens every time. What strikes an airline most is when the fuel price goes up, and in those first forty days or so of the war, it was very critical."He puts numbers on it. Fuel typically accounts for about 40 per cent of Malaysia Airlines' total operating cost. During the conflict, that share rose to nearly 55 or 56 per cent.For an airline already operating on slender margins, that is a brutal swing. He said the margin across the Asia-Pacific region averages only about 2 per cent. "If you sell $100, you only make $2 in profit. When something happens in some part of the world, that margin is gone."The Gulf's loss was Kuala Lumpur's gain, at least for a while. With the Middle East hubs disrupted, travellers who would normally have connected through the Gulf looked for other routes. Many of them, especially those travelling between Australia, New Zealand and Europe, turned to Southeast Asia."Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, in particular, saw a big increase in demand, and we increased our frequencies and our flights into London," he says. Load factors on those flights touched 95, 99 and even 100 per cent.That surge has since cooled. Demand plateaued around June or July, he says, because many of those who wanted to move had already done so. It is still strong, though. Loads to Europe remain in the high 80s to around 90 per cent.India: The market that keeps filling upThis is the first time in over two decades that he has visited Mumbai. Last time around, he had flown in as a pilot-in-command. When asked about the purpose of his visit, he said: "India is one of the biggest economies in the world, and I think India is the right market to go to."The numbers back him up. Malaysia Airlines operates about 80 flights a week to India, including 12 a week to Chennai, and flies to ten Indian destinations, among them both metros and second-tier cities. The airline carried about 1.3 million passengers on its India routes in the first half of 2025. Passenger growth in India is running at roughly 11 per cent year on year, and by the end of July the airline had already flown close to one million passengers on its India routes this year, he said.The planes are almost full. "Fortunately, or unfortunately, our load factor is right to the brim now." Loads on India routes average around 93 per cent. He cites 93 per cent in Chennai, 91 per cent in Mumbai and 91 to 92 per cent in most other cities, which he says makes India one of the highest-loading foreign markets in the network.How much of that traffic is bound for Malaysia? About 70 per cent of passengers from India travel onwards through Kuala Lumpur, and only about 30 per cent fly point to point. Most of the onward traffic is headed to Australia, mainly Sydney and Melbourne, with a smaller share going to Japan and very little to China, he said.That makes KL a hub in the true sense of the word, a role Capt Nasa is keen to push. “Kuala Lumpur is the fourth most connected hub in the world, ahead of Singapore and Bangkok,” he said. OAG data released in Sept put Istanbul airport at the first place globally with connections to 337 destinations worldwide, followed by London Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol in the third place. Kuala Lumpur retained its fourth position and remains the most connected airport in Asia, with destinations served increasing to 154.Bilaterals and poor inbound traffic from MalaysiaThe imbalance in India-Malaysia passenger traffic is stark, too. By his estimate, about 750,000 Indians travel to Malaysia, against roughly 200,000 Malaysians going the other way. That lop-sidedness is one reason capacity is hard to add. India's bilateral air services agreement caps what each side's carriers can fly, and Malaysia Airlines shares its Malaysian quota with AirAsia and Batik."Our work, through our government, is always about asking whether we can get more bilateral arrangements," he says. "The process is ongoing, and we have asked many times." He says he understands the position on both sides.The visa-free questionMuch of that growth in outbound traffic from India to Malaysia has come with a tailwind: Malaysia's visa-free regime for Indian travellers. It is due to lapse in December. He did not comment on whether it will be extended. "Our government-to-government relationship between Malaysia and India has been very strong, and I believe the visa-free arrangement benefits both countries."Malaysia has declared 2026 as Visit Malaysia Year, and the airline's own targets look to the same horizon. "We are looking at maybe two to three million tourists from India alone this year, across all carriers," he says. For an airline whose Indian planes are already nearly full, that number may be as much a message to the Malaysian government as a forecast.Profit, and the six-month checkIn April, the airline announced a profit of USD 34 million for 2025, roughly double the previous years. The CEO’s message back then was celebratory but cautious. He warned about volatility and geopolitics.So, six months on, which pressures have turned out to be more persistent or more severe than expected? The CEO said the first two months of the year were profitable and strong, financially, and operationally. Then he moved quickly to what he considers the airline's real achievement. Its on-time performance is running at 92 to 94 percent. "We are not only ensuring that we fly from A to B. We are selling an experience."He is clear-eyed about the ambition behind that. Malaysia Airlines now ranks 21st on Skytrax, up from 26th, and he wants it in the top ten within four years. "Can it be achieved? Obviously, it can."The fleet is the bottleneckThe more stubborn problem is supply. The airline ordered 95 aircraft three years ago and has received 29 so far. Another 66 are due over the next four years. Delays of three to five months are routine."I don't see the supply chain being resolved in the next five years, at least," he says. "I'm praying so hard for that, but looking at the trend, it might even take longer."For a small airline, the cost is high. Malaysia Airlines has already sold about 25 percent of its 2027 seats, he said. "If a flight is delayed by three months, a small airline like us has a big problem," he says. He is frank about the manufacturers. "We're trying our level best, and the manufacturers say they are doing theirs, but to me their level best is not good enough."The average age of the fleet is 10.3 years. He wants to bring it down to 5.7 by 2030, since about 75 per cent of the new order is replacement and only a quarter is growth. A decision on long-range widebody aircraft is expected within a month or two.“We should be announcing our white body replacement maybe next month or before year end, the replacement of our A350 aircraft, which is about nine years old today,” he said.When asked whether a passenger flying in 2030 can be sure of a fresh cabin, he declined to promise. "Nothing is certain. You will always have some aircraft that are ten years old. But I'm talking about the average."Premium, food and crewCapt Nasa describes the airline's long-term business plan, now in its third edition, as resting on four pillars: being a premium carrier, building partnerships, achieving operational excellence, and strengthening its non-airline businesses. Traffic isn’t the only goal. "We want to be known as a premium carrier, so everything we do is about driving premiumness, not just traffic."On the customer side, he narrows it to three things. The first is the cabin: new aircraft and, as importantly, cabins that work well.The second is food. "Malaysians love to eat, and Indians love to eat too," he says. He has added 30 menus in the last nine months, and the flight he took to India the day before the interview was serving an Indian menu. The airline will also build its own catering facility, with ground-breaking in July, to produce around 60,000 meals a day by 2028, selling the surplus to other airlines.When told that a passenger flying on a Malaysian carrier might prefer Malaysian food, he conceded the point but said the airline's own analysis shows that most customers want something familiar. So Indian food it is.The third is hospitality. “Malaysia Airlines' cabin crew have won a world's-best award seven times, and this year they are ranked third on Skytrax,” he said. The airline last topped the list about 18 years ago, and he believes it is on a path back to number one.Selling the stopoverBecause most Indian passengers are in transit, Malaysia Airlines has a product to coax them off the plane: the bonus side trip. A traveller who stops in Kuala Lumpur gets a free ticket to a second destination, a domestic destination."Say you are going to Japan. The price flying direct is one figure and the price through Kuala Lumpur is another, but we say, come through us and I will give you one ticket free to Langkawi."The offer has grown from six destinations to eight, including Kuching, Penang, Johor Bahru and Langkawi. It was introduced two or three years ago and is aimed at leisure travellers rather than corporate ones, who want to get to Australia, Japan etc directly, he said. The share of passengers who use it is small though, but it helps to sell, he added.On pricing, he insists the airline competes on something other than fares. "It is important for us to sell the experience. It is not about the price." Dynamic pricing, he adds, means early buyers can find fares cheaper than some competitors.Lessons from the pandemic“The learnings that we got from COVID is this. As an airline, you cannot put everything under one basket. So, when we restructured the company in 2023, we diversified our businesses. We've got airline business, we've got non-airline businesses, we want to be strong and to be resilient in our non-airline businesses,” he said. From the Indian market point of view, the airline sees cargo and MRO businesses as strong segments.With around 18,000 aircraft backlogged at manufacturers, airlines are extending leases, and that means more heavy checks, he said, adding that no Indian airline sends aircraft to Malaysia Airlines' MRO arm today. But he sees it as a chance, since the group works on both Boeing and Airbus. When told, India has long complained about losing maintenance business abroad, his answer was diplomatic: "To me, the cake is so big that everyone can have a portion." Cargo and MRO are two of the group's six non-airline businesses, along with loyalty, catering, ground handling and a training academy.Partners in code-shareMalaysia Airlines has a codeshare with IndiGo on six Indian domestic points and a joint business agreement with Singapore Airlines. It is also a Oneworld member, though that alliance has no Indian carrier. The CEO did not have passenger numbers for the IndiGo tie-up. “In terms of the number, it is steadily improving. It is not there yet, but we need it, we want it to be much better.”IndiGo's push into long-haul does not worry him unduly. Thirty or forty years ago, he notes, Southeast Asia and India had only six or seven airlines, and now there are more than 50. "Competition is stiff, but the market has grown a lot." He expects the Asia-Pacific region to grow six to seven per cent a year for the next 20 years, against about four per cent globally. "Of course, it is a concern to us. Even though the market is big, we have to be very smart."A smarter airlineTechnology, too, is on his list, as is with most airline CEOs. About 75 per cent of customers now start their search on Google or an AI tool, and about 20 percent of those convert into a ticket, he said. Malaysia Airlines runs 49 AI platforms across its operations, from flight planning to disruption management. Citing an example, he talks about rebooking disrupted passengers, where the system can use customer data to decide who goes on which flight, such as sending someone bound for London directly rather than through KL.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump establishes panel to probe Fed governor Lisa Cook in latest attempt to fire her
articles.summary: President Donald Trump established a committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook, in his latest attempt to fire her.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an order directing the attorney general and other top federal officials to establish a committee to investigate Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, in his latest attempt to fire her. “By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, I hereby establish a committee of inquiry (Committee) to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments,” read a presidential memorandum posted to the White House website. It said that the committee would “investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is ‘cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal.” “Governor Cook may submit a written position statement to the Committee regarding the allegations,” the memorandum said. The unprecedented White House announcement comes after a top White House official in August wrote a letter to Cook, saying that Trump was considering removing her from the Federal Reserve board. The White House memorandum said that Cook “shall appear at the hearing and be examined by the Committee,” as well as “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations.” The committee is set to meet Nov. 5 for the hearing, two days after the midterm elections. No president has ever fired a top Fed official. “In light of the President’s repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook — regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” said Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, Cook’s attorneys. “But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” Lowell and Eisen said they have engaged with the White House to determine if this is a “genuine” process and that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.” The memo follows a Supreme Court ruling in June, which allowed Cook to remain in her job for now. But the justices did not permanently block Trump from removing Cook, instead ruling that she had the right to an opportunity to defend herself. Trump’s latest move stems from allegations first leveled against Cook in August 2025 by Federal Housing Finance Agency chief Bill Pulte. Trump amplified those allegations on social media and, citing a “criminal referral” he said Pulte had sent to the Justice Department, attempted to remove her from the Fed’s board. Pulte alleged that Cook committed mortgage fraud, however documents obtained and reviewed by NBC News later revealed that Cook declared that the property in question was to be used as a “vacation home” and not her primary residence. The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Friday’s developments. Other top Trump administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, reportedly have similar mortgage situations. Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin have all called more than one property their “primary residence” on mortgage applications, according to a report last year from ProPublica. Cook, a governor on the Federal Reserve’s board, has a permanent vote on interest rates. Trump and Pulte’s attacks on Cook came amid a long-running pressure campaign by the administration to get the U.S. central bank to cut interest rates. “President Trump is convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank,” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, which oversees the Fed. “Instead of playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making, Trump should end the war in Iran and cancel his chaotic tariffs,” Warren said. Trump also recently resumed his attacks on another Fed governor, Jerome Powell. Trump claimed Sept. 30 that the former chairman was complicit in cost overruns for a construction project at the central bank’s headquarters. However, an inspector general’s report found no wrongdoing. Trump responded to the report by writing on social media, “He should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence.” Following the post, Attorney General Todd Blanche told Bloomberg News, “We’re not reopening a criminal investigation into him.” Powell has remained on the Fed’s board despite the end of his term as chair, breaking with tradition. As long as Powell remains on the board, the Trump administration is denied the opportunity to name a new board member of the president’s choice. Cook has consistently maintained that she did nothing wrong. Just weeks ago, Cook’s lawyer told the White House for a second time that, “There is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause.” “An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Abbe Lowell said Aug. 26. “These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will.” Lowell said he and Cook were prepared to continue to fight “any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.”

articles.title: Trump launches new effort to oust Fed Governor Lisa Cook
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is mounting a fresh offensive in his battle to oust Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, forming a committee of his own appointees to investigate allegations against her.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is mounting a fresh offensive in his battle to oust Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, forming a committee of his own appointees to investigate allegations against her. The committee will investigate alleged false statements Cook made in connection with mortgages on two properties and hold an in-person hearing at the White House on November 5, the White House announced on Friday. Newly installed Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, who is also serving as acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, is one of the three members. So is National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, a staunch defender of Trump’s economic agenda whom the president considered for Fed chair. The third member is Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Cook’s attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, said they have been in touch with the White House “to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise.” “Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” they said in a statement provided to CNN on Friday. The formation of the committee marks the latest salvo in Trump’s ongoing attempts to reshape the Fed and comes just weeks ahead of its next monetary policy meeting, where officials will consider whether interest rate changes are merited. Trump has long berated the politically independent Fed because it hasn’t lowered interest rates to his liking, publicly targeting Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell. But Trump has spared the current chairman, Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed to the position earlier this year after Powell’s term at the head of the central bank expired. Instead, Trump has insisted that Warsh is blocked by a “political” Board of Governors. The central bank’s eight-member Board votes on interest rate decisions, along with regional Fed presidents. While the Fed leader often plays an influential role in shaping the discussion on policy moves, decisions are ultimately the result of the 12-person committee process. At its September meeting, all 12 members, including Warsh, voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to contain inflation that has heated up largely due to the US war with Iran. Trump said later that Warsh shouldn’t have greenlit a rate hike. “I don’t blame Kevin Warsh. I probably would have voted against the Board if I were him,” Trump said in an interview Time Magazine published earlier this month. Separately, Trump reaffirmed he wants Warsh to “vote the way he wants.” Trump vs. Cook Trump previously sought to fire Cook over unproven allegations of mortgage fraud. Ultimately, in a 5-4 decision earlier this year, the Supreme Court ruled Trump could not immediately remove her. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his majority opinion released in June that Cook was entitled to sufficient time and notice to respond to a termination and that she wasn’t given a fair opportunity to respond last year when Trump initially sought to remove her. But that doesn’t mean Trump can’t lawfully fire her, he said. The law allows a president to remove Fed governors “for cause,” which is generally interpreted to mean negligence or malfeasance in the role. The “ultimate question of whether the presi­dent can remove Cook for cause will depend in part on the underlying facts,” Roberts wrote. “We have not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.” Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden in 2022 and is the first Black female Fed governor, with a term set to expire in 2038. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Americans’ feelings about the economy continue to worsen
articles.summary: Americans’ outlooks on the economy remain down in the dumps this month, new data released Friday showed.
articles.body: Americans’ outlooks on the economy remain down in the dumps this month, new data released Friday showed. The University of Michigan’s preliminary read on consumer sentiment for October showed its closely watched index falling to 46.3 from 48.1 last month. Consumers are wrangling with a high cost-of-living environment where inflation continues to run above normal and gas prices have soared higher in recent months as a result of the war in Iran. In September, borrowing got even more expensive when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years. If Friday’s lower-than-expected reading were to hold when the final data is released later this month, it would be the second-lowest level on record. The survey dates back to 1952, meaning Americans are feeling worse now than they did during the 1970s oil crisis, 9/11, the Great Recession, the Covid-19 pandemic and the inflation surge afterward. The five lowest-ever readings for the index all occurred within the past six months (with the record being set in May). “Frustration over cost-of-living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year,” Joanne Hsu, director of the university’s Surveys of Consumers, said in a statement. This story is developing and will be updated.

articles.title: Consumer sentiment falls to 5-month low as frustration mounts over higher costs
articles.summary: Americans are growing more concerned about higher borrowing costs.
articles.body:
Consumer sentiment fell in October as frustration over the higher cost of living weighed on Americans' views of the economy, according to a survey from the University of Michigan.

Overall consumer sentiment fell to 46.3 in October, down 1.8 points from September's reading of 48.1. The preliminary reading was slightly below Wall Street's expectation of 47.3.

"Frustration over cost-of-living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year," Joanne Hsu, the survey's director, said in the release.

With 25 days until the midterm elections, Hsu added that sentiment among Democrats and Republicans improved, but that was offset by a decline in independents.

Consumers face a growing number of macroeconomic concerns: Higher inflation; worries over the US national debt, which is now above $40 trillion ; and a rise in the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), which risks jumping to 6% for the first time since 2000. The 10-year yield is often a gauge for global borrowing costs, and its recent increase has dampened Americans' outlook for buying conditions.

This week, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate increased to 7.4% , a three-year high, according to Freddie Mac survey data.

Sentiment among groups who have fewer resources to weather price increases, such as lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios, declined this month.

As consumer prices rise and the war with Iran continues, Americans' outlook for inflation in the year ahead ticked up to 4.7% this month from 4.6% last month.

Inflation expectations were far higher than the 3.4% rate recorded in February, when the war in the Middle East and its subsequent energy shock began.

Gas prices have increased by more than $1.50 on average since the beginning of the war, according to AAA , and have stayed elevated above $4 since midsummer.

Long-term inflation expectations increased to 3.5% this month, a tick higher than the 3.4% reading in September. In recent months, they have consistently remained above the 2.8%-3.2% range seen in 2024.

articles.title: Adidas sues White Fox fashion label over four stripes design
articles.summary: Sportswear giant Adidas has filed a lawsuit against popular Australian online fashion brand White Fox Boutique for selling and promoting clothes featuring a four-stripe design that Adidas claims is deceptively similar to its own three-stripe trademark, CNN affiliate 7News reported.
articles.body: Sportswear giant Adidas has filed a lawsuit against popular Australian online fashion brand White Fox Boutique for selling and promoting clothes featuring a four-stripe design that Adidas claims is deceptively similar to its own three-stripe trademark, CNN affiliate 7News reported. In a filing lodged with the Federal Court of Australia on September 18, and seen by 7News, the German brand said it issued repeated requests to Sydney-based White Fox throughout 2026 to cease the sale of the clothes — all of which, it said, were rejected. White Fox, which was launched in 2013, is popular with teens and 20-somethings in Australia, the US and the UK, boasting more than 2.7 million followers on Instagram. Speaking in court in Sydney on Friday, Adidas’ barrister, Patrick Flynn, alleged that White Fox has been emblazoning its products with four stripes for months, 7News said. The lawyer also took issue with promotional material White Fox has circulated, the outlet reported, as the boutique’s clothes are often paired with genuine Adidas shoes. Flynn showed the court a campaign photograph of an influencer adorned in White Fox apparel and styled with Adidas footwear, 7News reported, demonstrating how the products’ proximity might confuse shoppers. “There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said. As well as the alleged trademark breach, Adidas is seeking damages from White Fox for what its lawyers said is White Fox “drawing an association in the minds of consumers.” Lawyers for White Fox denied all claims, arguing that other fast-fashion labels including Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein have also opted for a four-stripe look, 7News reported. “Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” White Fox’s barrister, Ed Heerey, told the court on Friday. “Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three,” he added. CNN has reached out to White Fox Boutique and Adidas for comment. Adidas has had a trademark on its three-stripe design in Australia since 1957, according to Australian government records. Back in 2013, it successfully sued Australian consumer goods and apparel company Pacific Brands because it sold shoes with a four-stripe design. Justice Ian Jackman slated the dispute for a hearing in early 2027.

articles.title: Flock offers voluntary separation packages to staff amid camera backlash
articles.summary: The automated license plate reader (ALPR) firm Flock Safety has offered employees voluntary separation packages ahead of its “next phase of growth,” as the firm faces mounting scrutiny from communities and policymakers across the country. “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for…
articles.body:
The automated license plate reader (ALPR) firm Flock Safety has offered employees voluntary separation packages ahead of its “next phase of growth,” as the firm faces mounting scrutiny from communities and policymakers across the country.

“Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth,” a spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement to The Hill on Friday.

The spokesperson emphasized this was not a layoff but a voluntary program that “reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”

Reuters, which first reported the packages , said the buyout program is expected to impact about 270 employees or about 18 percent of its staff. Flock declined to comment when asked about the percentages.

While there are various ALPR firms across the nation, Flock drew particular backlash this year for its network of more than 120,000 cameras across the country.

Flock’s plate readers record license plate numbers like traditional ALPRs, but can also record specific details about a car to create what the company calls a “ vehicle signature .” Recorded details include the make, model and color of the car along with unique features like bumper stickers, decals and accessories. It does not include facial recognition.

Privacy concerns have existed for years over ALPR technology, but Flock and other firms’ new use of AI and a series of recent news reports on law enforcement misusing the technology caught the attention of Capitol Hill this year.

Lawmakers from both parties have proposed legislation to limit the use of Flock and other ALPR technology. Last week, a group of progressive lawmakers including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) introduced legislation to ban federal agencies from using ALPRs.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled a bill last month called the Flock-Off Act, which would block any attempt to purchase, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities and localities. While the bill title references Flock, it would not be the only company impacted.

And Republican Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.) spearheaded a congressional hearing last month on AI-powered surveillance camera manufacturers as part of an investigation into Flock .

articles.title: Trump launches probe into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
articles.summary: Trump began efforts to remove Cook as one of the governors on the US Fed Reserve Board in 2025 and litigation is on.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has announced a committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and whether alleged false statements on mortgage documents constitute grounds for her removal under federal law.

The White House announced the new committee on Wednesday, but published the notice on its website on Friday.

The three-member committee, which will be tasked with reviewing evidence and reporting to the president on whether he has sufficient cause to remove her, will include the assistant to the president for economic policy, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the director of the Office of Government Ethics.

The notice says there will be a hearing on November 5, where Cook will be required to appear and answer questions.

Trump began efforts to remove Cook as one of the governors on the US Federal Reserve Board in August 2025 after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte accused her of misrepresenting two different properties on a 2021 mortgage application before she joined the central bank. She was appointed to the Fed Board in 2022 by then-President Joe Biden. Cook’s term runs until 2038.

Trump announced Cook’s removal amid the allegations , but Cook sued, and a federal judge blocked her firing in September 2025. Cook remained in office while the case continued.

In June, the Supreme Court declined to let Trump remove Cook while the litigation continues.

The case led to the US Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that the president could not remove a Fed governor without adequate cause and needed to follow a clear process to lay out the reasons and provide evidence.

The ruling left Cook in her position, but kicked the case against her back to a federal district court.

The case has been closely watched as Trump has put political pressure on the central bank to cut interest rates, including launching investigations into then-Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, whose term ended in May.

In December 2025, Trump said he would only appoint someone who agreed with him on cutting interest rates. He appointed Kevin Warsh as Powell’s replacement.

Amid ongoing tensions with Iran, pressure on the oil market and rising inflation, the Fed last month raised the benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75–4 percent, the first hike in three years. With the final rate decision before the midterm elections later this month, CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts that rates will likely remain unchanged.

articles.title: SpaceX's mobile play: The 'best argument just got weaker' for carriers
articles.summary: SpaceX's (SPCX) move to buy nationwide 800 MHz spectrum closes the biggest technical gap in its bid for a true mobile product. Wall Street believes the piece...
articles.body:
SpaceX's ( SPCX ) move to buy nationwide 800 MHz spectrum closes the biggest technical gap in its bid for a true mobile product. Wall Street believes the pieces are in place for Elon Musk's rocket and satellite company to make the move, but there's still a way to go.

The portfolio includes up to 14 MHz of paired low-band spectrum. In its announcement , SpaceX said the spectrum "addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US."

Once it receives final FCC approval, SpaceX said Starlink Mobile will combine its satellite-to-mobile constellation with "an advanced terrestrial deployment," using its 2 GHz mid-band spectrum for capacity and the 800 MHz band for coverage that reaches customers "even when they are in buildings." SpaceX noted, "most existing mobile devices already support this underused band."

Evercore ISI analyst Kutgun Maral, who rates SpaceX Outperform with a $230 price target, saw SpaceX's move as "the clearest signal yet that Starlink Mobile is moving from a wholesale coverage layer for carrier partners toward a credible direct-to-consumer US service."

"The carriers' best argument just got weaker," Maral wrote. He added that owning a coverage layer means SpaceX now negotiates any MVNO "from a stronger position."

Maral cautioned that the deal is "more of a coverage fix than a capacity solution." Even with EchoStar's 65 MHz, SpaceX would hold about 79 MHz of low- and mid-band spectrum in the US, vs. 280 to 380 MHz each for AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon.

SpaceX management has said that next-generation mobile satellites will begin flying in 2027, with full 5G-quality service capable of being turned on in the first half of 2028, according to Evercore.

Also this week, the FCC approved SpaceX's application to launch 15,000 Gen2 Starlink Mobile satellites, which the company says will deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of its current generation.

Mobile carriers like AT&T ( T ), T-Mobile ( TMUS ) and Verizon ( VZ ) slid on the news . Conversely, tower owners American Tower ( AMT ), Crown Castle ( CCI ) and SBA Communications ( SBAC ) rallied on hopes of future SpaceX terrestrial buildouts.

TD Cowen analyst Gregory Williams said the spectrum news "takes a back seat" to the release, which he said "intentionally used words like 'an advanced terrestrial deployment.'"

"We still believe SPCX wants an MVNO first; thus, SPCX could be bluffing," Williams wrote. "This could be a tactic, but taking SPCX on its word, this puts the carriers on notice."

articles.title: Four signs it is about to get uglier in the bond market as yields rise
articles.summary: By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Suzanne McGee and Laura Matthews NEW YORK, Oct 9 (Reuters) - It is white-knuckle time in the bond market.
articles.body:
By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Suzanne McGee and Laura Matthews

NEW YORK, Oct 9 (Reuters) - It is white-knuckle time in the bond market.

US Treasury yields have risen sharply since the war with Iran began in February, with the 10-year yield up some 135 basis points to 5.23% and the 30-year yield up around 110 basis points from its March ‌low to 5.614%. Both are trading at levels last seen more than two decades ago.

Investors are watching whether bond selling is starting to create its own momentum. Some key technical ‌measures suggest another surge to even-higher yields could be ahead, creating a feedback loop that amplifies the market stress, though there are also reasons to believe that buyers will soon step in, seeking to lock in yields at their most investor-friendly ​levels since George W. Bush was president.

"People in the market are recalibrating their expectations," said Dustin Reid, fixed income strategist at Mackenzie Investments.

Here are four signs that the selling could worsen.

Investors are seeking out protection against rising yields, referred to as the "payer skew," in the options market. Investors use these markets to insure their portfolios against a sharp move in yields without having to sell their Treasury holdings.

Demand for short-term protection against a jump in 10-year US swap rates has intensified, pushing the cost of insuring against a 200-basis-point rate rise over the next three months to 132 bps on Monday, the highest ‌since the March 2023 banking crisis triggered by the collapse of Silicon ⁠Valley Bank.

Swap rates refer to the cost investors pay to lock in a fixed interest rate instead of paying a floating rate.

While options are tied to swap rates rather than Treasury yields, the two typically move together, making the surge in payer skew an indication of concern about the risk of higher long-term ⁠Treasury yields.

Implied volatility, a key input in option prices, has climbed to 21.4 basis points for one-month options on 10-year swap rates, the highest since late March, reflecting growing uncertainty over the path of long-term yields.

A major contributor to the selloff has been a surge in corporate issuance to support the AI buildout, investors said. Spreads have remained tight, but buyers of longer-term bonds issued by AI hyperscalers are using the ​Treasury ​market to hedge their duration risk, a measure of exposure to rising interest rates — a practice that lately has ​spurred selling.

articles.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX just made a huge play to challenge the phone industry, and AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon stocks are getting crushed
articles.summary: Big move for Starlink!
articles.body:
Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) just sent a big message to the wireless industry: We want our piece of the subscriber pie.

Late Thursday, SpaceX said it will acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio. It positions Musk's satellite business Starlink to challenge legacy wireless giants across the US.

Shares of AT&T ( T ), T-Mobile ( TMUS ), and Verizon ( VZ ) tumbled on the news on Friday.

Concerns had already escalated across Wall Street that Starlink could disrupt legacy wireless operators like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile by transitioning from a rural broadband service into a direct mobile competitor.

Following its strategic acquisition of terrestrial spectrum and rapid deployment of advanced satellites, SpaceX had laid the groundwork to launch its own standalone cellular network alongside its direct-to-cell capabilities.

The expansion threatens traditional carriers' high-margin enterprise, emergency service, and rural subscriber bases, as well as lucrative international roaming revenues.

AT&T CEO John Stankey has taken notice of Starlink's moves, but hasn't lost sleep over it… yet.

"I think they're going to find places where they clearly have a good solution," Stankey told Yahoo Finance at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia conference in September . "In airlines and flights today, they have a fantastic broadband solution. In rural parts or territories, it's a very efficient way to get good bandwidth to people. I think we see that there's going to be some IoT-type applications, like connecting vehicles that are largely outdoors and maybe have line of sight to the sky, that they're going to have an opportunity to go in and do some things there that maybe we haven't done as effectively."

While Starlink will present competition, Stankey added, "there's also going to be the complementary dynamic of us being able to solve that other 2% of the use cases I talked about and bring our customers to those satellite operators, whether it be Amazon or SpaceX. They'll be the beneficiary of us aggregating that traffic and bringing it into the wholesale market to be able to be used."
